title: Sh-B-T
hookLine: Shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, to cease

cards: One morning in the book of Joshua, the people walk out of their tents and there's nothing on the ground. Through the wilderness journey, bread had come down from the sky and lay on the ground in the mornings.
Now they've crossed into the land and eaten its grain, and the text says it plainly: "And the manna ceased on the morrow." No miracle announced. No speech.
It just stopped. The verb for ceased is built from the same three letters as a word you already know, the name of a whole day of the week.

teach.b: You met it on day eleven as the oldest labor law; today, the root under it. First, creation. Genesis says God finished the work, "and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made."
Rested, in the English. In Hebrew, the verb is from this root: stopped, ceased. The text doesn't say God was tired.
It says the making stopped. Second, the opposite promise.

teach.h: DAY AND NIGHT SHALL NOT CEASE.
teach.b: After the flood, God tells Noah that "day and night shall not cease." The same root again. The world's rhythms never stop, and inside them, once a week, people do.
Third, who stops. The commandment in Exodus lists the son and the daughter, the servants, the animals, and "thy stranger that is within thy gates." Shabbat isn't a rest for those who can afford it.
Everyone in the household stops together.

Fourth, stopping is a skill. The rabbis of the Mishnah gave whole chapters to defining what counts as work on Shabbat, so stopping could be clear and shared, not a vague good intention. Notice the name.
The day isn't called after its meals, prayers or songs.
It's called after what people stop. Ceasing comes first, and the rest grows in the space it leaves.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat stop work from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and the rabbis' detailed categories of work, set out in the Mishnah and Talmud, guide what is set down for the day; practice varies across communities.

games.q: you've eaten the grain of the new land. the next morning you walk out of your tent. what's on the ground?
games.why: "And the manna ceased on the morrow." the verb is from Sh-B-T, the root of Shabbat.

practice: Put down whatever is in your hands, leave any open screen alone, and notice the urge to do the next thing without doing it.
Each time your mind starts making a list, let the list stop, the way the manna stopped: no speech, no fuss, just ceasing. If you pray, you can hold the word Shabbat on the breath, in and out.

wordCard.voice: Sh-B-T. Shin, bet, tav: to stop, to cease. The root of Shabbat, and of the manna that ceased. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Sabbath; from the root shin, bet, tav, to stop or cease.

carryVoice: Your line: to stop. The world keeps its rhythm, and once a week people step out of it. See you on the next root.
